title: Tencent's ORIDTP platform designs dual-target therapeutic peptides from scratch in Nature paper
subtitle: The paper, with Tencent's AI for Life Sciences Lab as first-listed affiliation, reports mouse experiments where AI-designed peptides cut tumor volume 94.2 percent and beat semaglutide at one-tenth the molar dose.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Nature published "De novo design of high-potency dual-target therapeutic peptides with ORIDTP" on November 25, with Tencent's AI for Life Sciences Lab as the first-listed affiliation. ORIDTP is a few-shot active-learning pipeline that generates candidate peptide sequences in silico, screens them with wet-lab feedback, and iterates. The paper covers two therapeutic programs: a metabolic program that hits the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors simultaneously, and an oncology program that blocks the immune checkpoints PD-1 and CTLA-4 with a single molecule. Both were designed from scratch rather than derived from existing peptide scaffolds.

The reported preclinical numbers are large. In obese mice, the lead dual-agonist candidate produced more weight loss than semaglutide or mazdutide at roughly one-tenth the molar dose. In a tumor model, the dual-checkpoint peptide IC-Dual.P3 reduced tumor volume by 94.2 percent versus a control group. These are mouse results, not human trial data, and the paper does not establish that either molecule would survive formulation, pharmacokinetic and toxicity testing in people — the stage at which most preclinical candidates fail.

What's new is less the targets than the method. GLP-1R/GCGR dual agonists are a known class, and PD-1/CTLA-4 is a workhorse combination in checkpoint inhibitor trials. The claim is that an AI system can design a single sequence that engages two receptors with the right geometry, without starting from a known lead, and that the hits translate from docking score to measured potency in animals. A 2024 Nature Chemistry paper from Cambridge and AstraZeneca got a sevenfold potency improvement on GCGR/GLP-1R dual agonists using a smaller machine-learning pipeline; ORIDTP's contribution is extending that approach to immune checkpoints and showing in vivo efficacy at that scale.

A note for learners: in AI-designed drug discovery, the number to watch is not the in vitro binding affinity or the in silico score — it is the in vivo result measured against the current standard of care. A 94.2 percent tumor reduction in a mouse model is a strong signal, but mouse oncology models are notoriously permissive and the clinical attrition rate from preclinical peptide to approved drug is above 90 percent. The platform matters more than any single molecule from it. If ORIDTP can keep producing hits across target classes, that is a general-purpose design capability; if it is one lucky peptide, it is a paper.
